     2	
     3	## Source
     4	https://climate.nasa.gov/vital-signs/carbon-dioxide/ and Our World in Data — CO₂ and Greenhouse Gas Emissions (Global Carbon Budget 2025)
     5	
     6	## Atmospheric CO₂ Concentration
     7	
     8	The latest measurement from NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory (February 2026) records atmospheric CO₂ at **429 parts per million (ppm)**. This represents a more than 50% increase from the pre-industrial baseline of approximately 280 ppm. The current level is at least 1.5 times greater than the natural increase observed at the end of the last ice age 20,000 years ago — a change that took thousands of years then but has occurred in roughly two centuries now. Ground-based and satellite measurements confirm the sharp acceleration, linked primarily to the burning of coal, oil, and natural gas.
     9	
    10	## Global Emissions Trajectory (1750–2024)
    11	
    12	Before the Industrial Revolution, CO₂ emissions were negligible. Growth remained relatively slow until the mid-20th century. In **1950**, the world emitted roughly **6 billion tonnes** of CO₂. By **1990**, emissions had nearly quadrupled to over **20 billion tonnes**. Today, global annual emissions from fossil fuels and industry exceed **35 billion tonnes**. While emissions growth has slowed in recent years, they have not yet peaked.
    13	
    14	![Annual CO₂ emissions by country](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    15	
    16	## Who Emits the Most? Country-Level Totals
    17	
    18	China is the world's largest emitter by a significant margin, producing over 12 billion tonnes annually — more than one-quarter of the global total. The United States peaked near 6 billion tonnes around 2005 and has since declined to roughly 5 billion tonnes. India has risen rapidly to approximately 3 billion tonnes. Europe's share has fallen substantially.
    19	
    20	| Country / Region | Approx. Annual CO₂ (billion t) | Share of Global | Trend (recent) |
    21	|---|---|---|---|
    22	| China | ~12.5 | ~27% | Slight increase |
    23	| United States | ~5.0 | ~14% | Declining |
    24	| India | ~3.0 | ~8% | Rising |
    25	| EU-27 | ~2.7 | ~7% | Declining |
    26	| Germany | ~0.6 | ~1.7% | Declining |
    27	| United Kingdom | ~0.3 | ~0.9% | Declining |
    28	| Brazil | ~0.5 | ~1.4% | Roughly stable |
    29	| France | ~0.3 | ~0.8% | Declining |
    30	
    31	In 1900, Europe and the US accounted for more than 90% of global emissions. By 1950, they still represented over 85%. Today, they account for less than one-third, while Asia — home to nearly 60% of the world's population — produces roughly half of all emissions. Africa and South America each contribute only 3–4%, comparable to international aviation and shipping combined.
    32	
    33	## Per Capita Emissions: Extreme Inequalities
    34	
    35	Per capita CO₂ emissions reveal stark global inequalities. The world's highest per capita emitters are major oil-producing nations with small populations (Qatar, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait). Among large, populous countries, the US, Australia, and Canada have per capita emissions roughly three times the global average.
    36	
    37	![Per capita CO₂ emissions over time](./assets/figure_1.jpg)
    38	
    39	| Country | Per Capita CO₂ (tonnes/year) |
    40	|---|---|
    41	| United States | ~15 |
    42	| Canada | ~13 |
    43	| Australia | ~15 |
    44	| South Africa | ~8 |
    45	| China | ~9 |
    46	| EU-27 | ~7 |
    47	| World average | ~5 |
    48	| United Kingdom | ~4 |
    49	| France | ~4 |
    50	| India | ~2 |
    51	| Kenya | <1 |
    52	| Chad / Niger | ~0.1 |
    53	
    54	The gap between the highest and lowest per capita emitters is approximately **150-fold**: the average American or Australian emits in under two days what the average person in Chad or Niger emits in an entire year. Importantly, countries with similar living standards can differ significantly — France and the UK have much lower per capita emissions than Germany or the Netherlands, largely because of their energy mix (higher nuclear and renewable shares).
    55	
    56	## 2024 Annual Change in Emissions
    57	
    58	The 2024 map of annual percentage change in CO₂ emissions shows a mixed picture. The United States and much of Europe recorded declines (roughly −1% to −5%), shown in blue. Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, and several African nations saw increases of +2% to +10% or more, shown in orange and red. Some countries in South America (notably one or two) experienced very large percentage increases (>10%), while others saw declines.
    59	
    60	![Annual percentage change in CO₂ emissions, 2024](./assets/figure_4.jpg)
    61	
    62	## Key Findings
    63	
    64	- **Global CO₂ emissions now exceed 35 billion tonnes per year** and have not yet peaked, despite slowing growth rates.
    65	- **China alone accounts for over 25% of global emissions** (~12.5 Bt), more than double the United States (~5 Bt); India (~3 Bt) is the third-largest and rising fast.
    66	- **The geographic center of emissions has shifted dramatically**: from >90% in Europe and the US in 1900 to Asia producing ~50% today, while the US and Europe combined are below one-third.
    67	- **Per capita inequalities are extreme** — a 150× gap separates the highest emitters (US, Australia at ~15 t/person) from the lowest (Chad, Niger at ~0.1 t/person).
    68	- **Energy mix and policy choices matter**: countries with similar prosperity levels (e.g., France vs. Germany) can have very different per capita emissions depending on their reliance on nuclear, renewables, or fossil fuels.

- **Style**: Top Consulting (Exhibit dark variant)

- **Tone**: Data-forward, analytical, authoritative — evoking McKinsey/BCG boardroom rigor

| Role | HEX | Purpose |
| ---- | --- | ------- |

| **Border/divider** | `#3A4150` | Card borders, divider lines, grid lines |

1	# Shared Technical Standards
     2	
     3	Common technical constraints for PPT Master, eliminating cross-role file duplication.
     4	
     5	---
     6	
     7	## 1. SVG Banned Features Blacklist
     8	
     9	The following features are **absolutely forbidden** when generating SVGs — PPT export will break if any are used:
    10	
    11	| Banned Feature | Description |
    12	|----------------|-------------|
    13	| `clipPath` | Clipping paths |
    14	| `mask` | Masks |
    15	| `<style>` | Embedded stylesheets |
    16	| `class` | CSS selector attributes (`id` inside `<defs>` is a legitimate reference and is NOT banned) |
    17	| External CSS | External stylesheet links |
    18	| `<foreignObject>` | Embedded external content |
    19	| `<symbol>` + `<use>` | Symbol reference reuse |
    20	| `textPath` | Text along a path |
    21	| `@font-face` | Custom font declarations |
    22	| `<animate*>` / `<set>` | SVG animations |
    23	| `<script>` / event attributes | Scripts and interactivity |
    24	| `marker` / `marker-end` | Line endpoint markers |
    25	| `<iframe>` | Embedded frames |
    26	
    27	---
    28	
    29	## 2. PPT Compatibility Alternatives
    30	
    31	| Banned Syntax | Correct Alternative |
    32	|---------------|---------------------|
    33	| `fill="rgba(255,255,255,0.1)"` | `fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.1"` |
    34	| `<g opacity="0.2">...</g>` | Set `fill-opacity` / `stroke-opacity` on each child element individually |
    35	| `<image opacity="0.3"/>` | Overlay a `<rect fill="background-color" opacity="0.7"/>` mask layer after the image |
    36	| `marker-end` arrows | Draw triangle arrows with `<polygon>` |
    37	
    38	**Mnemonic**: PPT does not recognize rgba, group opacity, image opacity, or markers.
    39	
    40	---
    41	
    42	## 3. Canvas Format Quick Reference
    43	
    44	### Presentations
    45	
    46	| Format | viewBox | Dimensions | Ratio |
    47	|--------|---------|------------|-------|
    48	| PPT 16:9 | `0 0 1280 720` | 1280x720 | 16:9 |
    49	| PPT 4:3 | `0 0 1024 768` | 1024x768 | 4:3 |
    50	
    51	### Social Media
    52	
    53	| Format | viewBox | Dimensions | Ratio |
    54	|--------|---------|------------|-------|
    55	| Xiaohongshu (RED) | `0 0 1242 1660` | 1242x1660 | 3:4 |
    56	| WeChat Moments / Instagram Post | `0 0 1080 1080` | 1080x1080 | 1:1 |
    57	| Story / TikTok Vertical | `0 0 1080 1920` | 1080x1920 | 9:16 |
    58	
    59	### Marketing Materials
    60	
    61	| Format | viewBox | Dimensions | Ratio |
    62	|--------|---------|------------|-------|
    63	| WeChat Article Header | `0 0 900 383` | 900x383 | 2.35:1 |
    64	| Landscape Banner | `0 0 1920 1080` | 1920x1080 | 16:9 |
    65	| Portrait Poster | `0 0 1080 1920` | 1080x1920 | 9:16 |
    66	| A4 Print (150dpi) | `0 0 1240 1754` | 1240x1754 | 1:1.414 |
    67	
    68	---
    69	
    70	## 4. Basic SVG Rules
    71	
    72	- **viewBox** must match the canvas dimensions (`width`/`height` must match `viewBox`)
    73	- **Background**: Use `<rect>` to define the page background color
    74	- **Line breaks**: Use `<tspan>` for manual line breaks; `<foreignObject>` is FORBIDDEN
    75	- **Fonts**: Use system fonts only (Microsoft YaHei, Arial, Calibri, etc.); `@font-face` is FORBIDDEN
    76	- **Styles**: Use inline styles only (`fill="..."` `font-size="..."`); `<style>` / `class` are FORBIDDEN (`id` inside `<defs>` is legitimate)
    77	- **Colors**: Use HEX values; for transparency use `fill-opacity` / `stroke-opacity`
    78	- **Image references**: `<image href="../images/xxx.png" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"/>`
    79	- **Icon placeholders**: `<use data-icon="icon-name" x="" y="" width="48" height="48" fill="#HEX"/>` (auto-embedded during post-processing)
    80	
    81	---
    82	
    83	## 5. Post-processing Pipeline (3 Steps)
    84	
    85	Must be executed in order — skipping or adding extra flags is FORBIDDEN:
    86	
    87	```bash
    88	# 1. Split speaker notes into per-page note files
    89	python3 scripts/total_md_split.py <project_path>
    90	
    91	# 2. SVG post-processing (icon embedding, image crop/embed, text flattening, rounded rect to path)
    92	python3 scripts/finalize_svg.py <project_path>
    93	
    94	# 3. Export PPTX (from svg_final/, embeds speaker notes by default)
    95	python3 scripts/svg_to_pptx.py <project_path> -s final
    96	# Default: generates native shapes (.pptx) + SVG reference (_svg.pptx)
    97	```
    98	
    99	**Prohibited**:
   100	- NEVER use `cp` as a substitute for `finalize_svg.py`
   101	- NEVER export directly from `svg_output/` — MUST export from `svg_final/` (use `-s final`)
   102	- NEVER add extra flags like `--only`
   103	
   104	**Re-run rule**: Any modification to `svg_output/` after post-processing has completed (including page revisions, additions, or deletions) requires re-running Steps 2 and 3. Step 1 only needs re-running if `notes/total.md` was also modified.
   105	
   106	---
   107	
   108	## 6. Shadow & Overlay Techniques
   109	
   110	> `<mask>` elements and `<image opacity="...">` are banned. Always use stacked `<rect>` or gradient overlays instead (see §2).
   111	
   112	### Shadow
   113	
   114	#### Filter Soft Shadow — Recommended
   115	
   116	Best for: cards, floating panels, elevated elements. `svg_to_shapes.py` automatically converts `feGaussianBlur` + `feOffset` into native PPTX `<a:outerShdw>`.
   117	
   118	```xml
   119	<defs>
   120	  <filter id="softShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
   121	    <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="8"/>
   122	    <feOffset dx="0" dy="4" result="offsetBlur"/>
   123	    <feFlood flood-color="#000000" flood-opacity="0.08" result="shadowColor"/>
   124	    <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   125	    <feMerge>
   126	      <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   127	      <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   128	    </feMerge>
   129	  </filter>
   130	</defs>
   131	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" filter="url(#softShadow)"/>
   132	```
   133	
   134	Recommended parameters:
   135	```
   136	stdDeviation:   6–10     (smaller = crisper, larger = softer)
   137	flood-opacity:  0.06–0.12  (keep low for a premium feel)
   138	dy:             3–6      (vertical > horizontal for natural top-light)
   139	dx:             0–2
   140	```
   141	
   142	#### Colored Shadow
   143	
   144	Best for: accent buttons, brand-colored cards. Use the element's own color family instead of black.
   145	
   146	```xml
   147	<filter id="colorShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
   148	  <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="10"/>
   149	  <feOffset dx="0" dy="6" result="offsetBlur"/>
   150	  <feFlood flood-color="#1A73E8" flood-opacity="0.20" result="shadowColor"/>
   151	  <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   152	  <feMerge>
   153	    <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   154	    <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   155	  </feMerge>
   156	</filter>
   157	```
   158	
   159	Replace `flood-color` with the element's brand color; keep `flood-opacity` between 0.12–0.20.
   160	
   161	#### Layered Rect Shadow — High-Compatibility Fallback
   162	
   163	Best for: maximum compatibility with older PowerPoint versions. Stack 2–3 semi-transparent rectangles behind the main card:
   164	
   165	```xml
   166	<!-- Shadow layers (back to front, largest offset first) -->
   167	<rect x="68" y="72" width="400" height="240" rx="16" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.03"/>
   168	<rect x="65" y="69" width="400" height="240" rx="14" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.05"/>
   169	<rect x="62" y="66" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#1A73E8" fill-opacity="0.04"/>
   170	<!-- Main card -->
   171	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
   172	```
   173	
   174	### Image Overlay
   175	
   176	#### Linear Gradient Overlay — Most Common
   177	
   178	Best for: image+text pages. Gradient direction should match text position (text on left → gradient darkens toward left).
   179	
   180	```xml
   181	<image href="..." x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"/>

   183	  <linearGradient id="imgOverlay" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="0">
   184	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.85"/>
   185	    <stop offset="55%"  stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.30"/>
   186	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0"/>
   187	  </linearGradient>
   188	</defs>
   189	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#imgOverlay)"/>
   190	```
   191	
   192	#### Bottom Gradient Bar
   193	
   194	Best for: cover slides and full-image pages with bottom title.
   195	
   196	```xml
   197	<defs>
   198	  <linearGradient id="bottomBar" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
   199	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0"/>
   200	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0.72"/>
   201	  </linearGradient>
   202	</defs>
   203	<rect x="0" y="380" width="1280" height="340" fill="url(#bottomBar)"/>
   204	```
   205	
   206	#### Radial Gradient Overlay — Vignette Effect
   207	
   208	Best for: full-screen atmosphere slides; draws attention to the center.
   209	
   210	```xml
   211	<defs>
   212	  <radialGradient id="vignette" cx="50%" cy="50%" r="70%">
   213	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0"/>
   214	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0.58"/>
   215	  </radialGradient>
   216	</defs>
   217	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#vignette)"/>
   218	```
   219	
   220	#### Brand Color Overlay
   221	
   222	Best for: slides needing strong visual brand identity.
   223	
   224	```xml
   225	<defs>
   226	  <linearGradient id="brandOverlay" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="0">
   227	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#005587" stop-opacity="0.80"/>
   228	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#005587" stop-opacity="0.10"/>
   229	  </linearGradient>
   230	</defs>

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1280 720">
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="topBar" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#C9A96E"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#E8C87A"/>
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>

  <!-- Background -->
  <rect width="1280" height="720" fill="#1A1D23"/>

  <!-- Top gradient bar -->
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="4" fill="url(#topBar)"/>

  <!-- Title -->
  <text x="60" y="52" fill="#E8E8E8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" font-weight="bold">
    Atmospheric CO₂ Reaches 429 ppm — 50% Above Pre-Industrial Levels
  </text>
  <line x1="60" y1="65" x2="1220" y2="65" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>

  <!-- Big stat callout -->
  <text x="640" y="220" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E8C87A" font-family="Arial Black, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="140" font-weight="bold">
    429
  </text>
  <text x="640" y="270" text-anchor="middle" fill="#C9A96E" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" font-weight="bold">
    parts per million
  </text>
  <text x="640" y="305" text-anchor="middle" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16">
    February 2026 · Mauna Loa Observatory (NOAA)
  </text>

  <!-- Three context cards -->
  <!-- Card 1 -->
  <rect x="60" y="360" width="360" height="200" rx="8" fill="#252A33" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="80" y="395" fill="#C9A96E" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">PRE-INDUSTRIAL BASELINE</text>
  <text x="80" y="430" fill="#E8E8E8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="36" font-weight="bold">~280</text>
  <text x="80" y="455" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">ppm (natural level)</text>
  <text x="80" y="490" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">Current level is >1.5× greater</text>
  <text x="80" y="515" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">than natural increase at the</text>
  <text x="80" y="535" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">end of the last ice age</text>

  <!-- Card 2 -->
  <rect x="460" y="360" width="360" height="200" rx="8" fill="#252A33" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="480" y="395" fill="#C9A96E" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">RATE OF CHANGE</text>
  <text x="480" y="430" fill="#E8E8E8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="36" font-weight="bold">~200 yrs</text>
  <text x="480" y="455" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">vs. thousands of years</text>
  <text x="480" y="490" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">A change that took millennia</text>
  <text x="480" y="515" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">now compressed into roughly</text>
  <text x="480" y="535" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">two centuries</text>

  <!-- Card 3 -->
  <rect x="860" y="360" width="360" height="200" rx="8" fill="#252A33" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="880" y="395" fill="#C9A96E" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">PRIMARY DRIVER</text>
  <use data-icon="factory" x="880" y="415" width="28" height="28" fill="#E8C87A"/>
  <text x="920" y="438" fill="#E8E8E8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold">Fossil Fuel Combustion</text>
  <text x="880" y="470" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">Coal · Oil · Natural Gas</text>
  <text x="880" y="500" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">Ground-based and satellite</text>
  <text x="880" y="525" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">measurements confirm the</text>
  <text x="880" y="545" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14">sharp acceleration</text>

  <!-- Timeline annotation -->
  <line x1="200" y1="600" x2="1080" y2="600" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="2"/>
  <circle cx="260" cy="600" r="6" fill="#3A4150"/>
  <text x="260" y="625" text-anchor="middle" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12">~280 ppm</text>
  <text x="260" y="640" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">Pre-industrial</text>

  <circle cx="640" cy="600" r="6" fill="#C9A96E"/>
  <text x="640" y="625" text-anchor="middle" fill="#C9A96E" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">1958</text>
  <text x="640" y="640" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">Keeling starts</text>

  <circle cx="1020" cy="600" r="8" fill="#E8C87A"/>
  <text x="1020" y="625" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E8C87A" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">429 ppm</text>
  <text x="1020" y="640" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">Feb 2026</text>

  <!-- Footer -->
  <line x1="60" y1="665" x2="1220" y2="665" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="60" y="690" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">Source: NOAA Mauna Loa Observatory · NASA Climate Vital Signs</text>
  <text x="1220" y="690" text-anchor="end" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12">02</text>
</svg>

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1280 720">
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="topBar" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#C9A96E"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#E8C87A"/>
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>

  <!-- Background -->
  <rect width="1280" height="720" fill="#1A1D23"/>
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="4" fill="url(#topBar)"/>

  <!-- Title -->
  <text x="60" y="52" fill="#E8E8E8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" font-weight="bold">
    Global Fossil Fuel CO₂ Emissions Grew Six-Fold: 6 Billion to 35+ Billion Tonnes
  </text>
  <line x1="60" y1="65" x2="1220" y2="65" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>

  <!-- Left: Line chart area -->
  <rect x="60" y="85" width="700" height="420" rx="8" fill="#252A33" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>

  <!-- Chart title -->
  <text x="80" y="110" fill="#C9A96E" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">GLOBAL CO₂ EMISSIONS TRAJECTORY (1750–2024)</text>

  <!-- Y-axis labels -->
  <text x="75" y="145" text-anchor="end" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">40</text>
  <text x="75" y="195" text-anchor="end" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">30</text>
  <text x="75" y="245" text-anchor="end" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">20</text>
  <text x="75" y="295" text-anchor="end" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">10</text>
  <text x="75" y="345" text-anchor="end" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">0</text>

  <!-- Grid lines -->
  <line x1="85" y1="140" x2="740" y2="140" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="0.5"/>
  <line x1="85" y1="190" x2="740" y2="190" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="0.5"/>
  <line x1="85" y1="240" x2="740" y2="240" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="0.5"/>
  <line x1="85" y1="290" x2="740" y2="290" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="0.5"/>
  <line x1="85" y1="340" x2="740" y2="340" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="0.5"/>

  <!-- Axis lines -->
  <line x1="85" y1="340" x2="740" y2="340" stroke="#6B7685" stroke-width="1"/>
  <line x1="85" y1="140" x2="85" y2="340" stroke="#6B7685" stroke-width="1"/>

  <!-- X-axis labels -->
  <text x="85" y="360" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">1750</text>
  <text x="250" y="360" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">1850</text>
  <text x="415" y="360" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">1900</text>
  <text x="580" y="360" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">1950</text>
  <text x="740" y="360" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">2024</text>

  <!-- Y-axis label -->
  <text x="30" y="240" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" transform="rotate(-90,30,240)">Billion tonnes CO₂</text>

  <!-- Line chart path (approximated trajectory) -->
  <polyline points="85,338 150,335 250,320 350,290 415,260 480,220 530,190 580,170 630,155 680,145 710,142 740,140" fill="none" stroke="#C9A96E" stroke-width="3"/>

  <!-- Key data point markers -->
  <circle cx="580" cy="170" r="5" fill="#E8C87A"/>
  <text x="580" y="155" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E8C87A" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold">~6 Bt</text>
  <text x="580" y="385" text-anchor="middle" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">1950</text>

  <circle cx="680" cy="145" r="5" fill="#E8C87A"/>
  <text x="680" y="130" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E8C87A" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold">~20 Bt</text>
  <text x="680" y="385" text-anchor="middle" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">1990</text>

  <circle cx="740" cy="140" r="6" fill="#EF5350"/>
  <text x="740" y="125" text-anchor="middle" fill="#EF5350" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">35+ Bt</text>
  <text x="740" y="385" text-anchor="middle" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">2024</text>

  <!-- Annotation -->
  <text x="80" y="420" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">Growth has slowed in recent years, but emissions have not yet peaked.</text>

  <!-- Right: figure_3.jpg reference -->
  <rect x="790" y="85" width="430" height="420" rx="8" fill="#252A33" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="810" y="110" fill="#C9A96E" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">ANNUAL CO₂ EMISSIONS BY COUNTRY</text>
  <image href="../images/figure_3.jpg" x="810" y="125" width="390" height="260" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"/>
  <text x="810" y="405" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12">Reference: figure_3.jpg — Country-level annual</text>
  <text x="810" y="422" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12">emissions showing China's steep rise post-2000</text>
  <text x="810" y="439" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12">and the US decline from its ~6 Bt peak.</text>

  <!-- Bottom stat bar -->
  <rect x="60" y="530" width="380" height="80" rx="8" fill="#252A33" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="80" y="560" fill="#C9A96E" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">1950</text>
  <text x="80" y="585" fill="#E8E8E8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" font-weight="bold">~6 Bt</text>
  <text x="80" y="602" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12">Baseline year</text>

  <rect x="460" y="530" width="380" height="80" rx="8" fill="#252A33" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="480" y="560" fill="#C9A96E" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">1990</text>
  <text x="480" y="585" fill="#E8E8E8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" font-weight="bold">~20 Bt</text>
  <text x="480" y="602" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12">Nearly quadrupled</text>

  <rect x="860" y="530" width="360" height="80" rx="8" fill="#252A33" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="880" y="560" fill="#C9A96E" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">2024</text>
  <text x="880" y="585" fill="#EF5350" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" font-weight="bold">35+ Bt</text>
  <text x="880" y="602" fill="#A0AAB8" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12">Still rising</text>

  <!-- Footer -->
  <line x1="60" y1="665" x2="1220" y2="665" stroke="#3A4150" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="60" y="690" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">Source: Global Carbon Budget 2025</text>
  <text x="1220" y="690" text-anchor="end" fill="#6B7685" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12">03</text>
</svg>

# 01_cover

Welcome to this data-driven briefing on global CO₂ emissions. Over the next eight minutes, we will trace the arc of carbon emissions from the Industrial Revolution to 2024 — examining who emits, how the map has shifted, and the stark inequalities that shape climate negotiations.

Key points: (1) Scope covers 1750–2024 (2) Audience: policy analysts and climate negotiators (3) Sources: Global Carbon Budget 2025, NASA
Duration: 30 seconds

---

# 02_atmospheric

[Transition] Before examining who emits, let's establish the atmospheric reality we are operating within.

The latest measurement from NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory records atmospheric CO₂ at 429 parts per million — a more than 50% increase from the pre-industrial baseline of approximately 280 ppm. [Pause] To put this in context: the natural increase observed at the end of the last ice age 20,000 years ago took thousands of years. We have achieved a comparable change in roughly two centuries. [Data] 429 ppm versus 280 ppm — this is not a marginal shift; it is a fundamental alteration of Earth's atmosphere. The driver is unambiguous: the burning of coal, oil, and natural gas.

Key points: (1) 429 ppm Feb 2026 — 50%+ above pre-industrial (2) Rate of change unprecedented in geologic record (3) Fossil fuel combustion is primary driver
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 03_global_trajectory

[Transition] With that atmospheric context, let's examine the trajectory of emissions themselves.

Before the Industrial Revolution, CO₂ emissions were negligible. Growth remained relatively slow until the mid-20th century. In 1950, the world emitted roughly 6 billion tonnes. By 1990, emissions had nearly quadrupled to over 20 billion tonnes. [Benchmark] That is a six-fold increase in four decades. Today, global annual emissions from fossil fuels and industry exceed 35 billion tonnes. [Data] The critical point: while growth has slowed in recent years, emissions have not yet peaked. The curve is still rising, even if the slope is flattening.

Key points: (1) 6 Bt → 20 Bt → 35+ Bt trajectory (2) Growth slowed but no peak yet (3) Post-2000 acceleration driven by Asia
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 04_china_surpasses

[Transition] Understanding the global trajectory is essential, but climate policy operates at the national level. Let's examine who emits the most today.

China is the world's largest emitter by a significant margin, producing over 12.5 billion tonnes annually — more than one-quarter of the global total. [Benchmark] That is more than double the United States at roughly 5 billion tonnes. The United States peaked near 6 billion tonnes around 2005 and has since declined. India has risen rapidly to approximately 3 billion tonnes and is still climbing. Europe's share has fallen substantially — EU-27 now emits roughly 2.7 billion tonnes, about 7% of the global total. [Scan Room] The shifting rankings are not just statistics; they redefine negotiating positions in international climate forums.

Key points: (1) China ~12.5 Bt, ~27% global (2) US peaked ~2005, now declining (3) India rising fast to ~3 Bt (4) Europe's share fallen substantially
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 05_regional_shift

[Transition] These national totals reflect a deeper structural transformation: the geographic center of global emissions has shifted dramatically.

In 1900, Europe and the United States accounted for more than 90% of global emissions. By 1950, they still represented over 85%. [Data] Today, they account for less than one-third, while Asia — home to nearly 60% of the world's population — produces roughly half of all emissions. [Benchmark] That is a complete inversion of the global emissions map within a single century. Africa and South America each contribute only 3–4%, comparable to international aviation and shipping combined. This shift is structural, not cyclical, and it has profound implications for burden-sharing in climate agreements.

Key points: (1) 1900: Europe+US >90% (2) 2024: Asia ~50%, US+Europe <33% (3) Africa & South America ~3–4% each (4) Structural, not cyclical shift
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 06_per_capita

[Transition] Total emissions tell one story; per capita emissions tell another — and for climate equity, this is the more consequential narrative.

Per capita CO₂ emissions reveal stark global inequalities. Among large, populous countries, the United States and Canada have per capita emissions roughly three times the global average. [Data] The gap between the highest and lowest per capita emitters is approximately 150-fold. The average American or Australian emits in under two days what the average person in Chad or Niger emits in an entire year. [Benchmark] World average is approximately 5 tonnes per person. The US is at ~15, China at ~9, EU-27 at ~7, India at ~2, and Chad/Niger at ~0.1. These disparities are central to debates over climate justice and differentiated responsibilities.

Key points: (1) 150× gap highest to lowest (2) US ~15 t vs Chad/Niger ~0.1 t (3) World average ~5 t (4) Per capita central to equity debates
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 07_annual_change_2024

[Transition] Let's turn from historical patterns to the most recent annual data — what happened in 2024?

The 2024 map of annual percentage change in CO₂ emissions shows a mixed picture. The United States and much of Europe recorded declines of roughly −1% to −5%. [Data] However, Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, and several African nations saw increases of +2% to +10% or more. Some countries in South America experienced very large percentage increases exceeding 10%. [Benchmark] There is no uniform global direction — emissions are declining in some major economies while rising in others. For negotiators, this means the aggregate global trajectory remains upward even as individual regions decarbonize.

Key points: (1) US/Europe: −1% to −5% (blue) (2) Russia/SE Asia/Africa: +2% to +10%+ (orange/red) (3) No uniform global direction (4) Aggregate still rising
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 08_energy_mix

[Transition] A critical question for policy is: what drives these differences? The answer lies in energy mix.

Countries with similar living standards can have very different per capita emissions depending on their energy sources. [Benchmark] France and the United Kingdom have much lower per capita emissions than Germany or the Netherlands — largely because of their energy mix. France derives the majority of its electricity from nuclear power. The UK has aggressively expanded offshore wind. Both have reduced fossil fuel dependency. Germany, by contrast, phased out nuclear and retains significant coal capacity. The Netherlands relies heavily on natural gas. [Data] The result: France and the UK emit roughly 4 tonnes per person, while Germany and the Netherlands are significantly higher. This proves that policy choices — not just prosperity — determine carbon intensity.

Key points: (1) France/UK: high nuclear + renewables, ~4 t/person (2) Germany/Netherlands: higher fossil share, significantly higher per capita (3) Policy choices matter as much as GDP
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 09_key_takeaways

[Transition] Let me synthesize these findings into five key takeaways for your negotiations and policy work.

First, global emissions exceed 35 billion tonnes and have not yet peaked — despite slowing growth rates. Second, China alone emits more than 25% of the global total, more than double the US, with India rising fast. Third, per capita inequalities remain extreme — a 150-fold gap separates the highest from lowest emitters. Fourth, the US and Europe are declining, but historical cumulative responsibility remains large; the geographic center has shifted to Asia. And fifth, policy and energy mix choices — not just prosperity — determine per capita outcomes. France versus Germany is the proof. [Pause] The data is clear. The question for negotiators is how to translate these realities into equitable, effective agreements. Thank you.
